1.title: Cost-Optimized Compute
1.text: Welcome to Module twelve: Cost-Optimized Compute. This module covers task statement four point two, the second task of Domain four, Design Cost-Optimized Architectures. You will choose among On-Demand, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances and Spot, right-size instances, scale and stop what is idle, use serverless and containers, and pick a load balancer. The exam describes a usage pattern and asks for the cheapest fit.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Choose among On-Demand, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances and Spot. Design Spot workloads that survive interruptions. Right-size with instance families, sizes, Graviton and Compute Optimizer. Pick scaling, hibernation, serverless and container options that cut cost. And choose a load balancer and an availability level that match the workload class.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lantern and Loom Trims the Compute Bill
1.text: The compute bill at Lantern and Loom is too high. The web tier runs all day at a steady baseline, with spikes at sales. Nightly image processing can be restarted if it stops. Test servers sit idle evenings and weekends. Large instances run at ten percent of C P U. And each team runs its own load balancer. Your job is to cut the bill without hurting the shop.

1.title: EC2 Purchasing Options
1.text: There are four main ways to buy E C two capacity. On-Demand has no commitment and bills per second, so it suits short, unpredictable or new workloads. Savings Plans commit you to a dollar amount per hour for one or three years, which suits steady usage that needs flexibility. Reserved Instances commit you to a specific configuration for one or three years, for steady usage that will not change. Spot Instances need no commitment, but they can be interrupted, so they suit fault-tolerant, flexible work at up to ninety percent off. Dedicated Hosts and Capacity Reservations serve licensing and capacity, not price. Exam tip: steady baseline means commit; spiky or new means On-Demand; restartable work means Spot.

1.title: Savings Plans and Reserved Instances
1.text: Here is how the commitment types compare. Compute Savings Plans save up to sixty-six percent and apply to any instance family, size, operating system, tenancy and Region, and also to Fargate and Lambda. E C two Instance Savings Plans save up to seventy-two percent, for one family in one Region, with any size, operating system or tenancy. Standard Reserved Instances save up to seventy-two percent for one configuration, and can be sold on the R I Marketplace. Convertible Reserved Instances save up to sixty-six percent and can be exchanged by hand. You can pay all, partial or no upfront, and the terms cannot be cancelled. Savings Plans give no capacity reservation and do not cover Spot. Exam tip: most flexibility means Compute Savings Plans; deepest discount for one family means an E C two Instance plan.

1.title: Layering Purchase Options
1.text: Think of demand in layers. The figure shows three bands over a daily demand curve. The bottom band is the minimum you always use, covered by Savings Plans or Reserved Instances. The middle band is predictable peaks, served by On-Demand. The top band is restartable bursts, served by Spot. Never commit to the peak, because unused commitment is still billed. Commit to the minimum you always use, and let the layers above flex with demand. Exam tip: commit to the floor of your usage, not the ceiling.

1.title: Spot Instances Done Right
1.text: Spot saves a great deal, but only when the design allows for interruption. Use it for stateless, fault-tolerant work such as batch, continuous integration, containers, big data and rendering. Be flexible across instance types and Availability Zones, so there are more capacity pools to draw from. Use an Auto Scaling group or an E C two Fleet with the price-capacity-optimized strategy, which picks available, low-price pools. Handle the two-minute interruption notice with Event Bridge, to checkpoint or drain. Turn on Capacity Rebalancing to replace instances at elevated risk early. Do not use Spot for stateful or tightly coupled work. Exam tip: restartable and flexible means Spot; a database or a single critical server is never Spot.

1.title: Right-Sizing and Instance Families
1.text: Match the family and the size to the work. General purpose instances, M and T, balance C P U and memory, and T is burstable, for web servers and small databases. Compute optimized, C, has high C P U, for batch and encoding. Memory optimized, R and X, has large memory, for caches and in-memory databases. Storage optimized, I and D, has high local I O, for warehouses and No S Q L. Accelerated, P and G, has graphics processors, for machine learning. Graviton instances, built on Arm, often cost less for the same work. Match size to measured use, not to a guess. Exam tip: instances at ten percent C P U are too big, so right-size instead of buying more commitment.

1.title: Compute Optimizer and Cost Visibility
1.text: A W S Compute Optimizer reads fourteen days of metrics and flags resources as over-provisioned, under-provisioned or optimized. It covers E C two, Auto Scaling groups, E B S, Lambda, E C S on Fargate and more. Enhanced infrastructure metrics, a paid feature, extend the look-back to ninety-three days. Cost Explorer adds rightsizing and Savings Plans recommendations. Right-size first, then commit, because a plan on oversized instances locks in waste. Opt in at the organization level to see all accounts. Budgets alert on Savings Plans coverage, cost allocation tags and consolidated billing share commitments across teams, and the Cost and Usage Report gives line items. Exam tip: right-size first, commit second.

1.title: Scaling for Cost
1.text: Scaling choices change cost. Horizontal scaling adds and removes instances, so capacity follows demand and you pay only for what runs. Vertical scaling uses a larger size and needs a restart, so it fits one-off right-sizing. Scheduled scaling scales in before known quiet periods. Target tracking holds a metric, such as fifty percent C P U. Stopping non-production servers nights and weekends removes the instance charge, though E B S still bills. Mixed instances groups blend On-Demand and Spot. Exam tip: for idle test servers, schedule them off; for spikes, scale horizontally, not with a larger instance.

2.title: Hibernation and Availability by Workload Class
2.text: Match availability to the workload class. Production needs Multi-A Z, Auto Scaling and a committed baseline. Non-production can run in a single A Z, and be stopped or scaled to zero off hours. Batch and analytics can run on Spot and restart on interruption. Hibernation saves memory to the encrypted E B S root volume, then stops the instance. On start, memory and processes return, so an application that is slow to warm up resumes fast. There is no instance charge while hibernated, and you pay for E B S storage, including the saved memory. The instance must be enabled for hibernation at launch, with limits on size and days. Exam tip: to stop at night but keep in-memory state, hibernate the instance.

2.title: Serverless and Containers
2.text: Each compute service bills differently. Lambda charges for requests and duration, by memory in gigabyte seconds; set memory by testing, and Arm Graviton costs less per millisecond. Fargate charges for v C P U and memory per second, with no servers; use Fargate Spot for restartable tasks and right-size the task. E C S or E K S on E C two bills for the instances, so pack containers densely and use Spot and Savings Plans. Plain E C two bills for instance time, and is best for steady, high utilization. Compute Savings Plans cover E C two, Fargate and Lambda, and containers suit microservices. Exam tip: spiky, or idle most of the day, means Lambda or Fargate; always busy means E C two with a commitment.

2.title: Hybrid, Edge and Licensing
2.text: Hybrid and edge options exist for requirements, not for price. A W S Outposts puts A W S infrastructure on premises, for low latency or data residency. Local Zones and Wavelength put compute close to users, or inside five G networks. Edge processing, with CloudFront Functions or Lambda at Edge, cuts work at the origin. License Manager tracks license rules and prevents overuse. Dedicated Hosts let you bring your own per-socket or per-core licenses. Optimize C P Us lowers the v C P U count to cut per-core licensing cost. Use hybrid and edge only when a requirement demands it. Exam tip: do not add Outposts for price; it exists for latency or residency.

2.title: Load Balancer Cost Strategy
2.text: Pick the balancer by layer, then control how many you run. The Application Load Balancer works at layer seven, for H T T P and H T T P S, host and path rules, and many apps on one balancer. The Network Load Balancer works at layer four, for T C P and U D P, static I P addresses and extreme scale. The Gateway Load Balancer works at layer three, for inline firewall and inspection appliances. Billing is hourly plus capacity units used. Consolidate many apps behind one Application Load Balancer, with host and path rules and separate target groups. Delete idle balancers, because they bill by the hour. Exam tip: each team with its own A L B is the clue; consolidate with host or path routing.

2.title: Choosing the Cheapest Compute
2.text: Here is the chooser. The figure branches from the workload pattern to the purchase option and service. Steady and always on means Savings Plans or Reserved Instances. Spiky or new means On-Demand with Auto Scaling. Restartable and flexible means Spot. Idle most of the day means Lambda or Fargate. Idle at night with memory to keep means hibernate. Exam tip: name the usage pattern first, then pick the cheapest option that tolerates it.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Cost-Optimized Compute
2.text: Here is what the exam asks. Which purchase option fits a steady, spiky or restartable workload. Which Savings Plan or Reserved Instance gives the needed flexibility. How to right-size, and with which tool. Which service is cheapest: E C two, Lambda or Fargate. And which load balancer to use, and how to consolidate. Exam tip: look for the clues: steady, restartable, idle, flexible, on premises and per team.

2.title: Design Check: Lantern and Loom Trims the Compute Bill
2.text: Here is the Design Check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. A steady, all-day web tier: Compute Savings Plans for the baseline. Sale-day spikes: On-Demand through Auto Scaling. Restartable nightly image jobs: Spot in a mixed-instances group. Idle test servers: a scheduled stop, or hibernate to keep state. Large instances at ten percent C P U: Compute Optimizer, then right-size or move to Graviton. A load balancer per team: one A L B with host and path rules. And to commit safely: right-size first, then commit.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. To buy, commit to the floor with Savings Plans, use On-Demand for peaks, and Spot for restartable work. For Spot, be flexible across types and zones, use price-capacity-optimized, and expect a two-minute notice. To right-size, use families, sizes, Graviton and Compute Optimizer, and then commit. To run less, schedule servers off, hibernate, and use Lambda or Fargate when idle. And to balance, consolidate behind one A L B, and use Outposts only for latency or residency.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Lantern and Loom runs a nightly image-processing job that splits work into many small tasks. The job can restart any task if an instance stops. The team wants the lowest compute cost. Which approach fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: an Auto Scaling group that uses several instance types and Spot Instances. Restartable, flexible work suits Spot, and several types give more capacity pools.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. The Lantern and Loom web tier runs steadily all day. The team may move from C five to Graviton instances next year, and may later move some services to Fargate. They want a commitment discount without being tied to one family. Which purchase fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: a Compute Savings Plan. It applies across families, Regions and Fargate and Lambda, so the discount follows the move.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Which two statements about Spot Instances and Savings Plans are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Compute Savings Plans also apply to Fargate and Lambda usage, and a Spot Instance gets a two-minute interruption notice before it is reclaimed. Savings Plans cannot be cancelled, Spot has no guaranteed run time, and Savings Plans do not discount Spot.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A Lantern and Loom reporting server takes twenty minutes to load data into memory each morning. It is idle every night. The team wants to pay no instance charge overnight and still resume with the memory loaded. What should they do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: hibernate the instance at night and start it in the morning. Memory is saved to the encrypted E B S root volume, so the instance charge stops.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Several Lantern and Loom instances run at about ten percent C P U. The architect wants data-driven size recommendations across all accounts before buying any commitment. What should they use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: enable A W S Compute Optimizer for the organization. It analyzes utilization and recommends right-sized resources, and a commitment on oversized instances would lock in waste.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all five answers. Question one: A. Question two: D. Question three: B and E. Question four: C. Question five: B. In Module thirteen, we cut the cost of databases.
